defaults.permitted_development: A wraparound extension in England only stays within permitted development if the side and rear elements both satisfy Class A at the same time. In practice, many wraparound layouts need planning permission because the combined footprint, width or boundary effect stops the scheme being a simple side or rear addition. In villages and open-edge settings, bulk, roof form and how the addition sits in wider views often matter as much as the headline measurements.

rules.height_rules: Single-storey wraparound elements should stay within the usual Class A height limits, with particular care on the side return where the 3m eaves rule can apply close to a boundary.
rules.depth_rules: The rear leg must meet the normal rear-extension depth rules, while the side leg still has to remain subordinate to the original house. One part of the design cannot compensate for the other.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary relationships matter on both arms of a wraparound extension. The side return is often the tightest point, while the rear corner can create a stronger overbearing effect than a straight rear wall of the same depth. In villages and open-edge settings, bulk, roof form and how the addition sits in wider views often matter as much as the headline measurements.
rules.roof_rules: Keep the roof simple and subordinate. A joined-up roof that creates a bulky mass around the rear corner is less likely to stay within the simpler householder route.
rules.materials_rules: Use materials that match or sit comfortably with the existing house so the combined side-and-rear form does not read as an oversized add-on. In villages and open-edge settings, bulk, roof form and how the addition sits in wider views often matter as much as the headline measurements.

rules.permitted_development: A wraparound extension only counts as permitted development if the side and rear elements both satisfy the Class A rules together. In practice many wraparound layouts need planning permission because the combined footprint stops being a simple rear or side addition. In villages and open-edge settings, bulk, roof form and how the addition sits in wider views often matter as much as the headline measurements.

rules.height_rules: In Amber Valley, stepped roof forms matter more than headline measurements, because broad plots can still make a wraparound extension look like a second house wing if the roof rises too confidently.
rules.depth_rules: The rear leg still has to meet the normal rear-extension depth rules, and the side leg must remain proportionate to the original house. A wraparound layout cannot borrow tolerance from one element to excuse the other.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary relationships matter on both arms of the extension. The side return is often the pinch point, while the rear corner can create a stronger overbearing effect than a straight rear wall of the same depth. In villages and open-edge settings, bulk, roof form and how the addition sits in wider views often matter as much as the headline measurements.
rules.roof_rules: Keep the roof simple and subordinate. Joined-up roofs that create a large boxy mass around the rear corner are more likely to need permission than a clearly secondary arrangement.
rules.materials_rules: External materials should match or sit comfortably with the existing house so the combined side-and-rear form does not look like an overgrown add-on. In villages and open-edge settings, bulk, roof form and how the addition sits in wider views often matter as much as the headline measurements.

restrictions.conservation_area: Extensions in a conservation area often need a tighter design and siting assessment, especially on visible elevations or where the scheme would alter roof form, frontage or the rhythm of the street.
restrictions.listed_building: Do not rely on standard householder permitted development rights for a listed building. Listed building consent is usually required for works affecting character, and planning permission may also be needed.
restrictions.article4_notes: Article 4 directions can remove the usual householder fallback route in selected streets or heritage areas, so check the property's designation before relying on permitted development.

restrictions.listed_building: Our experienced team deals with applications to build new properties or change the use of existing buildings; they also offer pre-application advice for prospective developers. Our officers deal with other types of permissions too, such as works to listed buildings, protected trees or applications for advertisements.
restrictions.article4_notes: We may also have removed some of your permitted development rights by issuing an 'Article 4' direction. This will mean that you have to submit a planning application for work which normally would not need one.
